items.name: narration_en
items.direction: Narrate this as a popular geography YouTube Shorts channel. The Narrator is a deep, warm, confident storyteller: brisk and curious, with natural emphasis and a short comic pause before each punchline; a touch of wonder for the deep-sea lines. Chars voices funny cartoon characters, short and punchy.
lines: You could sink Everest in this hole... with two kilometres to spare.
And after a hundred and fifty years, we still can't say how deep it is.
[nervous giant mountain, deep booming voice, gulping] Wait. I'm going IN there?
This is the Challenger Deep, about three hundred kilometres from Guam.
Rewind to eighteen seventy-five. Sailors on H M S Challenger lowered a weighted rope.
It hit bottom at eight thousand, one hundred and eighty-four metres. The deep still carries their ship's name.
[proud Victorian sailor, hearty, then a small unsure pause] Deepest spot on Earth! ...Probably.
Then came sonar. Nineteen fifty-one: ten thousand, eight hundred and sixty-three metres. Nineteen fifty-seven, a Soviet ship: eleven thousand and thirty-three.
That's half an Eiffel Tower... of disagreement.
Sonar doesn't measure depth. It times an echo... then uses the speed of sound.
And in seawater, that speed changes with temperature, salt and pressure.
Guess the speed wrong... and the bottom moves.
[tiny bouncy sonar ping, high and chirpy, defensive] Don't look at me. I just bounce.
And the bottom isn't one point. It's three narrow basins.
So this year, a Japanese team mapped it again, with five sound-speed models.
Best answer: ten thousand, nine hundred and twenty-seven metres. The models alone disagreed by eighteen.
The twist? In nineteen eighty-four, a Japanese ship got ten thousand, nine hundred and twenty.
Forty-two years later... the answer moved seven metres.
The deepest point on Earth isn't a number. It's a range.
[nervous giant mountain, deep booming voice, worried] So how far down am I going?
This is Bhoogol. Follow for more Geography Fun Facts.
